title: The outside of your body: what each part does and how to care for it

summary.text: Your two thumbs grew from the same genes, yet their fingerprints are different. Your skin, hair, nails, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, hands, feet and private parts are external organs: body parts you can see, each with its own job. Many of them have guards that people mistake for dirt, such as earwax, nose mucus and eyelashes. The top layer of your skin is dead cells, and new skin keeps growing underneath to replace it. Each part needs its own care, and washing hands with soap is one of the most important habits of all.
summary.art: A child standing with arms out, with small labelled circles around them: an eye with lashes, an ear, a nose, teeth, a fingertip with swirling ridges, a foot, and a strip of skin flaking.

intro.hook: Press your thumb onto a clean glass or a steel tumbler. Now breathe on that spot. A swirly pattern appears. That is your thumbprint. Nobody has ever been found with the same one, not even an identical twin.
intro.text: Your skin left that mark without you trying. Sweat comes out of tiny holes along the ridges of your fingertips. Your fingers also pick up a little oil from your face and hair. So everything you touch keeps a faint copy of your ridges. Every outside part of your body has a job like this. Some parts have guards that most people think are dirt. And every part needs its own kind of care.
intro.art: A child's thumb pressed on a steel tumbler, then a misty breath showing a swirling fingerprint on the shiny steel.

outcomes: I can name the external organs (skin, hair, nails, eyes, ears, nose, mouth and teeth, hands, feet and private parts) and say the job of each one.
I can give two ways to care for each external organ, and the reason for each way.
I can wash my hands and brush my teeth the right way, and explain from my own test why soap matters.
I know the correct names of my private parts and how to keep them clean. I know my body belongs to me, which touches are not OK, and who my trusted adults are.
I can explain that hair, nails and the outer skin are made of dead cells pushed out by living cells underneath, and that my outer skin keeps renewing itself.
I can explain why earwax, eyelashes, nose hairs and mucus are helpers, not dirt, and why we never poke things into ears, eyes or noses.
I can say what scientists agree on about our outer body, and what they still argue about, such as what fingertip ridges are for and whether we can be too clean.
I can compare my two thumbprints and explain why they are different, though they grew from the same genes.

terms.meaning: A part of the body that does a special job.
terms.example: Your eyes are organs for seeing. Your skin is an organ that covers and protects you.
terms.art: An eye, an ear and a hand, each with a small job label.

terms.meaning: An organ on the outside of the body, which you can see.
terms.example: Your nose, ears, hands and skin are external organs.
terms.art: A child's outline with the outside parts glowing.

terms.meaning: An organ inside the body, which you cannot see.
terms.example: Your heart and lungs are internal organs. They are inside your chest.
terms.art: A child's outline with a faint heart and lungs drawn inside.

terms.meaning: The stretchy covering of the whole body. It is the biggest organ you have.
terms.example: Skin keeps water in and dirt out. It lets you feel a hot cup.
terms.art: A hand holding a warm steel cup, with the skin shown in a zoom-in circle.

terms.meaning: The tiny living building block that bodies are made of. It is far too small to see with your eyes.
terms.example: Your skin is made of millions of cells, packed together like bricks in a wall.
terms.art: A zoom-in from a hand to tiny packed cells like bricks.

terms.meaning: A tough material that hair, nails and the top layer of skin are made of.
terms.example: Your nails, a cow's horns and a bird's feathers are all made of keratin.
terms.art: A fingernail, a cow's horn and a feather side by side.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes in the skin. Sweat comes out through them.
terms.example: On a hot day, sweat comes out of your pores and makes your forehead wet.
terms.art: A zoom-in of skin with tiny holes and sweat drops.

terms.meaning: Salty water that comes out of your skin. It cools you down as it dries.
terms.example: After playing in the sun, your shirt gets wet with sweat.
terms.art: A child after running, with drops on the forehead.

terms.meaning: The eyelid is the flap of skin that closes over the eye. Eyelashes are the short hairs on its edge. They keep dust out.
terms.example: When dust blows, you blink and your lashes catch it.
terms.art: A close-up of an eye half closed, with lashes catching a speck of dust.

terms.meaning: Salty water that keeps your eyes wet and washes dust away.
terms.example: When smoke gets in your eyes, they fill with tears.
terms.art: An eye with a tear washing a speck to the corner.

terms.meaning: A sticky wax made inside the ear, usually yellow-brown. It traps dust and tiny germs, and slowly moves out by itself.
terms.example: A little wax at the opening of your ear is normal. Wipe it with a cloth.
terms.art: A side view of an ear canal with wax slowly moving outwards.

terms.meaning: A thin skin stretched across the inside of the ear. Sound makes it shake, so you can hear.
terms.example: A cotton bud or a hairpin pushed into the ear can tear the eardrum.
terms.art: A drawing of an ear canal ending in a thin drum-like skin.

terms.meaning: The slippery, sticky liquid inside your nose. It traps dust and germs.
terms.example: When you have a cold, your nose makes extra mucus.
terms.art: A nose with tiny hairs and sticky mucus catching dust specks.

terms.meaning: The hard, shiny outside layer of a tooth. It is the hardest material in your body.
terms.example: Enamel lets your teeth crunch a raw carrot or a peanut.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half, showing a shiny white outer layer.

terms.meaning: Your first set of teeth. There are 20 of them. They fall out one by one, and bigger teeth grow in their place.
terms.example: A wobbly front tooth at age 6 or 7 is usually a milk tooth getting ready to fall out.
terms.art: A smiling child with a gap where a milk tooth fell out.

terms.meaning: The pattern of tiny ridges on the tip of each finger. Every finger has its own pattern, and no two people have been found to share one.
terms.example: Your thumb leaves a fingerprint on a shiny steel tumbler.
terms.art: A big swirling fingerprint with its ridges clear.

terms.meaning: Instructions inside almost every cell of your body, passed down from your parents. They guide how your body grows.
terms.example: Genes help decide the colour of your eyes and whether your hair is curly or straight.
terms.art: A child between two parents, with a tiny zoom-in circle of a cell holding a coiled thread.

terms.meaning: Tiny living things, too small to see, that can make us ill.
terms.example: Germs on dirty hands can get onto food, and then into your tummy.
terms.art: A hand under a magnifying glass with tiny specks shown on the skin.

terms.meaning: A cleaner that grabs onto oil and grease. Water then washes the oil, and the germs stuck in it, away.
terms.example: Plain water does not wash oily hands clean. Soap does.
terms.art: Soapy hands under a tap, with bubbles.

terms.meaning: The habits that keep our body clean, so that we stay healthy.
terms.example: Washing hands before eating is good hygiene.
terms.art: A child washing hands before a meal of rice and dal.

terms.meaning: The parts of the body covered by underwear. They are used to pass urine and stool. They are private: they belong to you.
terms.example: Boys have a penis. Girls have a vulva. These are their correct names, like elbow or knee.
terms.art: A simple outline of a child wearing underwear and a vest, with the underwear area shaded.

terms.meaning: A grown-up you know well, who listens to you and keeps you safe.
terms.example: A parent, a grandparent, an aunt or a teacher can be a trusted adult.
terms.art: A child talking to a kind grown-up who is listening, kneeling at the child's height.

terms.meaning: Tiny insects that live in hair and lay eggs called nits. They crawl from head to head.
terms.example: Lice make your head itchy. A fine comb and special shampoo get rid of them.
terms.art: A fine-toothed comb going through hair, with a small insect drawn large in a circle.

explanations.description: Look in a mirror. Everything you can see is on the outside of you. Your skin, hair, nails, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, teeth, hands, feet and private parts are your external organs. Each one does a job. Under your skin are the internal organs, like the heart, lungs, stomach and brain. They have their own unit. The outside parts and the inside parts work together all the time. Your nose takes in air, and your lungs inside use it.
examples: Your eyes see a ball coming. Your hands catch it. Your feet run to it.
Your nose smells food cooking. Your mouth starts to make spit, ready to eat.
Your skin feels cold. You put on a sweater.
explanations.art: A child in front of a mirror, with the outside parts labelled, and a faint outline of the heart and lungs inside.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: the parts of the body we can see, and how they differ from the parts inside.
explanations.definition: An organ is a body part with its own job. External organs are on the outside of the body, where we can see them. Internal organs are inside.

explanations.description: Spread out flat, a grown-up's skin would cover about one door. Skin has many jobs. It keeps water inside you, so you do not dry up. It keeps dirt and most germs out. It lets you feel touch, heat, cold and pain. When you are hot, sweat comes out through tiny holes called pores, and you cool down as it dries. In sunlight, skin also makes vitamin D, which your bones need. To care for skin, bathe every day, dry the folds well, and cover cuts. Stay in the shade in the hottest part of the day.
examples: A bandage on a cut keeps dirt out while the skin mends itself.
Your fingertips can feel a single grain of rice in your palm with your eyes shut.
After a bath, drying between your toes and under your arms stops itchy rashes.
explanations.art: A child's skin in a zoom-in circle, with labels: keeps water in, keeps germs out, feels, sweats.
explanations.context: Your skin covers all of you. This card explains its many jobs, and how to look after it.
explanations.definition: Skin is the stretchy covering of the whole body. It is the biggest organ of the body.

explanations.description: You cannot feel it, but you are shedding skin all the time. Tiny flakes fall off every day. Some of the dust in a house is made of these flakes. New skin is always growing underneath, so the outer layer is replaced about every month or two. This is why a scraped knee heals and a sunburn peels. Bathing washes away the old flakes, with sweat and dirt. Scrubbing hard does not help. It can hurt the new skin underneath.
examples: Clear sticky tape pressed on your arm picks up tiny white flakes. Those are dead skin cells.
A scraped knee grows new skin over a week or two.
After a sunburn, the top skin peels off in sheets.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of skin like layers of a cake: new cells at the bottom, flat old cells at the top flaking off.
explanations.context: This card is about how your skin replaces itself. You can see it in the sticky tape test.
explanations.definition: The top layer of skin is made of flat, dead cells. New cells are always being made underneath. They push up, and the old ones flake off.

explanations.concept: Hair and nails: dead, yet growing
explanations.description: Why does a haircut not hurt? Because the hair you can see has no nerves. Living cells at the root, under the skin, keep making new hair and push the old hair out. Hair grows about 1 centimetre a month. Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month. Toenails grow about half as fast. Hair keeps your head warm and shades it from the sun. Eyebrows stop sweat dripping into your eyes. Nails protect your fingertips and help you pick up small things. To care for them, wash and comb your hair. Cut nails short and straight, and keep them clean, because dirt and germs hide under long nails.
examples: Your hair grows back after a haircut, but the cut never hurts.
A cut fingernail grows long again in a few weeks.
Biting nails puts the germs from under them straight into your mouth.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a finger showing the living root of the nail under the skin and the dead nail pushing out, and the same for a hair.
explanations.context: This card explains why haircuts and nail cutting don't hurt, and how hair and nails grow.
explanations.definition: Hair and nails are made of keratin, a tough material made by living cells. The part you can see is dead. Only the root, under the skin, is alive.

explanations.description: Your eyes are soft and easy to hurt, so they have many guards. Your eyebrows stop sweat and rain running into them. Your eyelashes catch dust. Your eyelids blink shut in a flash when something comes close. Each blink spreads tears over the eye, keeping it wet and washing dust away. To care for your eyes, never rub them hard. If something gets in, blink and wash with clean water. Read in good light, and look far away often. Never look at the sun, not even for a moment.
examples: When a ball flies at your face, your eyes shut before you decide to shut them.
Onion juice in the air makes your eyes fill with tears.
Playing outdoors and looking far away is good for children's eyes.
explanations.art: An eye with arrows: eyebrow turning sweat aside, lashes catching dust, lid blinking, tears washing.
explanations.context: This card is about how your eyes are protected, and how you can help protect them.
explanations.definition: The eyes are the organs of sight. Eyelids, eyelashes, eyebrows and tears are their guards.

explanations.concept: Ears and the wax that cleans them
explanations.description: The outer ear is shaped like a funnel to catch sounds. Sounds travel down a short tube, the ear canal, to the eardrum. The eardrum is a thin skin, a little like the skin of a drum. Sound makes it shake, and that is how you hear. The ear canal makes wax. The wax traps dust and tiny germs. Then it slowly moves outwards by itself, helped by your jaw moving when you chew and talk. So ears mostly clean themselves. Doctors say never put cotton buds, hairpins or matchsticks into your ears. They push wax deeper and can tear the eardrum. Don't pour oil in either, unless a doctor tells you to. Just wipe the outside with a cloth. Keep away from very loud sounds.
examples: A little wax at the opening of the ear is normal. Wipe it off with a towel after a bath.
Chewing roti moves your jaw, which helps the wax move out.
Loud music through earphones for a long time can hurt hearing.
explanations.art: A side cut-away of an ear: the funnel, the canal with wax moving outwards on a little conveyor, and the eardrum.
explanations.context: This card explains how ears hear and how they keep themselves clean.
explanations.definition: The ears are the organs of hearing. Earwax traps dust and germs in the ear canal, and slowly carries them out.

explanations.concept: Nose: air, smell and a dust trap
explanations.description: Air comes into your body through your nose. Inside, short hairs and sticky mucus catch dust, pollen and germs, so less of it gets deep inside you. The nose also warms and wets the air. And it smells. Smell tells you when food is cooking or when milk has gone bad. To care for your nose, blow it gently into a handkerchief or tissue, one side at a time. Do not pick it, because fingers carry germs in. When you sneeze, sneeze into your elbow or a handkerchief, so your germs don't fly onto other people.
examples: After a dusty day, the mucus you blow out is dark. Your nose caught that dust.
When you have a cold, food tastes dull, because you can't smell it well.
Sneezing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands.
explanations.art: A nose cut-away with tiny hairs and mucus catching dust specks as air flows in.
explanations.context: This card is about the nose, and how it stops dust and germs getting inside you.
explanations.definition: The nose is the organ for breathing in air and for smelling. Hairs and sticky mucus inside it trap dust and germs.

explanations.description: Children have 20 milk teeth. From about age 6, they fall out one by one, and bigger teeth grow in. A full grown-up set has 32 teeth. Front teeth cut and bite. Back teeth grind food, like a grinding stone. Teeth are covered in enamel, the hardest material in your body. But tiny germs in your mouth feed on sugar and make acid. The acid slowly eats holes in the enamel. To care for your teeth, brush twice a day, for about two minutes. Brushing at night matters most, because your mouth makes less spit while you sleep. Spit helps protect teeth. Rinse your mouth with water after eating, and keep sweet sticky food for mealtimes.
examples: A toffee stuck between your teeth feeds mouth germs for hours.
Front teeth cut a guava. Back teeth grind it.
Saying 'ta ta ta' needs your tongue to tap behind your top teeth.
explanations.art: A smiling mouth with front teeth labelled 'cut' and back teeth labelled 'grind', and a toothbrush.
explanations.context: This card is about the mouth and teeth, and why brushing at night matters most.
explanations.definition: The mouth takes in food and water. Teeth bite and chew food. The tongue tastes, moves food and helps us talk.

explanations.description: Your thumb can turn and touch the tip of every finger. This lets you hold a pencil, a needle or a single grain of rice. Your fingertips are packed with nerves, so they feel very well. On their skin are tiny curving ridges. Sweat comes out of tiny holes along the ridges, and your fingers pick up oil from your face and hair. So you leave fingerprints on what you touch. Hands also pick up germs from everything they touch. So wash them with soap before eating, after the toilet, after playing outside and after touching animals. Rub every part for at least 20 seconds, then rinse. Hands carry a thin layer of oil and grease, and germs stick in it. Soap grabs that oil, and water carries it away.
examples: You leave fingerprints on a glass, a mirror and a phone screen.
Germs from a door handle can get onto your roti if you don't wash your hands.
A blind reader feels the raised dots of Braille with the fingertips.
explanations.art: Two soapy hands, with the steps of handwashing in small pictures around them: palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, nails.
explanations.context: This card is about hands: what they do, the ridges on the fingertips, and why we wash them with soap.
explanations.definition: The hands hold, feel and make things. Fingertips have ridges that make our fingerprints. Hands touch everything, so they carry germs.

explanations.description: The bottom of each foot curves up a little in the middle. This curve is called the arch. It works like a spring when you walk and run. Feet sweat a lot, especially inside shoes. Wet, warm skin between the toes can get itchy rashes. Some tiny worms in damp soil can get in through bare skin. To care for your feet, wash them every day and dry well between the toes. Wear chappals or shoes outside, especially near drains or wet soil. Cut toenails straight across.
examples: A wet footprint on a dry floor shows the arch. The middle of the print is thin.
Shoes worn all day without socks often smell, because of sweat and germs.
Chappals protect your feet from hot roads, glass and germs in mud.
explanations.art: A child's wet footprint on a stone floor, the thin middle showing the arch, next to a pair of chappals.
explanations.context: This card is about feet: what they do and how to keep them healthy.
explanations.definition: The feet carry the whole weight of the body. They help us stand, balance, walk and run.

explanations.concept: Private parts: clean, private and yours
explanations.description: These parts have correct names, just like elbow or knee. Using the right names is not rude. It helps you tell a doctor or a grown-up clearly if something hurts. To keep them clean, wash them every day when you bathe. After the toilet, clean yourself with water or toilet paper, from front to back. Then wash your hands with soap. Wear clean, dry underwear every day. Private parts are also private. Your body belongs to you. Nobody should touch your private parts, or ask to see them, or ask you to touch theirs. The only exceptions are a parent helping to keep you clean, or a doctor checking you, with your trusted grown-up there. If any touch feels wrong or confusing, it is never your fault. Say no, get away and tell a trusted adult. Secrets about touching should never be kept.
examples: A doctor checks a child's tummy pain while the child's mother stays in the room.
A child tells their aunt about a touch that felt wrong, and the aunt listens and helps.
A clean pair of underwear every morning stops itching and rashes.
explanations.art: A simple outline of a child in vest and underwear, a hand raised to say 'stop', and a trusted grown-up nearby listening.
explanations.context: This card is about the private parts: their names, how to keep them clean, and the rules that keep you safe.
explanations.definition: Private parts are the parts of the body covered by underwear. Boys have a penis and girls have a vulva. Both have a bottom, with an opening called the anus. They are used to pass urine and stool.

explanations.concept: Little guards that look like dirt
explanations.description: Many people think earwax and mucus are just dirt to dig out. In fact, they are traps. Dust and germs stick to them, and the body moves them out. Eyelashes and eyebrows look like decoration, but they guard the eyes. Even the tiny ridges on your fingertips may help you grip and feel. Good care means helping the guards, not fighting them. Wipe the outside. Never poke in.
examples: Earwax moves out of the ear by itself, like a slow conveyor belt.
Mucus traps dust, and you blow it out.
Tears wash a speck of dust to the corner of your eye.
explanations.art: A team picture: an eyelash, an eyebrow, a blob of earwax, a nose hair and a tear drawn as guards around a sleeping child.
explanations.context: This card explains why some parts that look like dirt are really there to protect you.
explanations.definition: Earwax, nose mucus, eyelashes, eyebrows and tears are guards. They trap dirt, wash it away or keep it out.

explanations.description: Everyone agrees that fingertips have ridges, and that every person's pattern is different, even an identical twin's. Each of your ten fingers has its own pattern too, so even your two thumbs differ. The ridges form before you are born, between about 10 and 16 weeks in the womb. They grow from a deeper layer of skin, so after a scrape the same pattern grows back. But what are the ridges for? Scientists still argue.
examples: Pressing your fingertips on a wet steel plate, you can still feel and grip it.
Running your fingertip over cloth, you can tell cotton from silk with your eyes shut.

perspectives.explanation: Many people thought ridges help us grip, like the grooves on a tyre. In 2009, a test in Britain found that on smooth, dry surfaces, ridges actually grip a little less. They may still help grip on rough or wet things, by letting water escape.
In 2009, scientists in France built a fake fingertip with ridges. When it slid over a surface, the ridges made tiny shakes that helped it sense fine textures. So ridges may help us feel.
Some scientists think ridges do several jobs at once. Some think they help skin stretch without tearing. Nobody is sure yet.

explanations.art: A fingertip in a zoom-in circle, with ridges like the lines on a ploughed field, and question marks.
explanations.context: This card is about the swirly ridges on your fingertips. Scientists know they are unique, but they still argue about what they are for.

explanations.description: Washing hands with soap stops many illnesses. Everyone agrees on that. But millions of tiny living things, too small to see, live on our skin all the time, and many of them help us. Some scientists ask whether children who meet very few germs grow up with more allergies. This is still being studied.
examples: Washing hands before eating stops many tummy illnesses. Doctors agree on this.
Children who grow up on farms, around animals and soil, seem to get some allergies less often.

perspectives.explanation: He noticed that children with more older brothers and sisters got hay fever less often. He wondered if catching more germs early helped. This became known as the hygiene hypothesis.

He argued that what matters is not catching colds, but meeting the 'old friends': harmless microbes from soil, animals and other people that humans have always lived with. Washing hands before eating does not take these away.
Keep washing hands with soap at the important times. Also play outdoors, in soil and around plants and animals. The two go together.

explanations.art: A child with soil on their hands from a potted plant, next to a sink with soap, with a balance scale between them.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: is it possible to be too clean?

agreed.text: Each external organ has its own job, and the organs work together.
agreed.evidence: When one part is hurt, its job suffers. A blocked nose makes food taste dull, and cold, numb fingers fumble with buttons. People who cannot see often learn to read Braille with their fingertips, so another part takes on some of the work.

agreed.text: The outer skin keeps renewing itself, and hair and nails grow from living roots.
agreed.evidence: Sticky tape picks up dead skin flakes from anyone's arm. Cut hair and nails grow back, while the cut part never hurts.

agreed.text: Washing hands with soap stops many germs spreading.
agreed.evidence: In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis made doctors in a Vienna hospital wash their hands in a chlorine solution, and far fewer mothers died. Many studies since have shown handwashing with soap cuts tummy and chest illnesses.

agreed.text: Sugar helps mouth germs make acid that damages teeth, and brushing with fluoride toothpaste protects them.
agreed.evidence: Children who eat sweet snacks often get more holes in their teeth. Dentists see fewer holes in children who brush twice a day.

agreed.text: Every finger has its own print, and fingerprints form before birth.
agreed.evidence: Police have compared millions of fingerprints for over 100 years. No two have been found to match, not even those of identical twins, or the two thumbs of one person.

challenging.claim: Earwax is dirt, so ears should be cleaned out with cotton buds.
challenging.who: Many people believe this. Cotton buds are sold everywhere.
challenging.for: Wax looks dirty. Taking it out feels clean.
challenging.against: Ear doctors say wax protects the ear and moves out by itself. Cotton buds push wax deeper and can hurt the eardrum. Only a doctor should remove wax that is stuck.
challenging.context: This card is about a common habit of cleaning ears, and why ear doctors say not to.

challenging.claim: Shaving or cutting hair makes it grow back thicker and darker.
challenging.who: A common belief in many homes, including about shaving a baby's head.
challenging.for: Short new hair feels rough and looks dark against the skin.
challenging.against: Cutting only removes the dead part. The living root under the skin does not change. Mildred Trotter, an American scientist, tested this in 1928. She and later scientists found that shaved hair grows back the same.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea about haircuts, and what tests found.

challenging.claim: Reading in dim light ruins your eyes for good.
challenging.who: Many parents and grandparents have said it.
challenging.for: Reading in dim light makes your eyes tired and sore.
challenging.against: Eye doctors say dim light makes eyes tired, but it does not cause lasting harm. Studies suggest children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become short-sighted.
challenging.context: This card is about a warning many children hear, and what eye doctors now think.

challenging.claim: No two fingerprints in the world can ever be the same.
challenging.who: Police and courts have often treated this as certain.
challenging.for: No two people have ever been found with the same prints, even twins.
challenging.against: Nobody can check every person. Also, smudged prints can be matched wrongly. In 2004, the FBI wrongly matched a man's fingerprint to a bombing in Spain, and later said sorry.
challenging.context: This card is about how sure we can be that fingerprints are unique, and how a match can go wrong.

challenging.claim: The more you scrub and wash, the healthier you are.
challenging.who: Many soap and cleaner advertisements suggest this.
challenging.for: Handwashing really does stop many illnesses.
challenging.against: Scrubbing skin hard can hurt it. Many helpful microbes live on skin. Some scientists think children also need to meet harmless microbes from soil, animals and people.
challenging.context: This card asks whether cleaner is always better.

challenging.claim: Old Indian ways of cleaning teeth, with neem twigs and a tongue scraper, are just old habits.
challenging.who: Some people think only toothpaste and brushes work.
challenging.for: Toothpaste with fluoride is very well tested for protecting teeth.
challenging.against: Ancient books like the Charaka Samhita describe cleaning teeth with twigs and scraping the tongue. Some studies found neem twigs do reduce mouth germs. Many dentists say a twig used well cleans, but fluoride toothpaste protects enamel best.
challenging.context: This card is about the datoon, a twig used to clean teeth in India for over two thousand years.

big_questions.q: Your hair and nails are dead, but they are part of you. Is a part of you still 'you' if it is not alive?
big_questions.hint: Think about a haircut. Is the hair on the floor still yours?

big_questions.q: Your skin is replaced every month or two. Are you the same person you were last year?
big_questions.hint: What stays the same when the cells change?

big_questions.q: Why would a body make earwax and mucus, which look like dirt?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to dust if nothing stopped it at the door?

big_questions.q: Where exactly do you end and the world begin? At your skin? At the air you breathe out?
big_questions.hint: You leave fingerprints and skin flakes everywhere you go.

big_questions.q: Your two thumbs have the same genes, and so do identical twins. Why are their prints still different?
big_questions.hint: Think about how each fingertip grows before you are born.

big_questions.q: Who decides who can touch your body?
big_questions.hint: Is your body yours even when you are small?

big_questions.q: In the past, some people were made to clean toilets and drains for everyone else, and were treated unfairly. Who keeps your town clean today, and how are they treated?
big_questions.hint: Think of the people who sweep your street. Do you know their names?

big_questions.q: If you had no sense of touch, what would be dangerous?
big_questions.hint: Think of a hot tava, or a sharp stone in your shoe.

big_questions.q: Is a person who cannot see or hear any less a whole person?
big_questions.hint: What do people do when one sense is missing?

story.title: Ruksana's Ink Thumbs
story.note: Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose were real. They worked in Calcutta in the 1890s for Edward Henry, the head of the Bengal police, on a way to sort fingerprints. Haque worked out much of its counting. The system was taken up in British India in 1897 and later in Britain, and it was named after Henry. Ruksana, her family and everything they say and do are imagined.
text: In the city of Calcutta, in the year 1896, a girl called Ruksana had the dirtiest thumbs in her lane.

It was not her fault. Her uncle, Azizul Chacha, brought work home. Every evening he came up the stairs with a bundle of cards tied in string. Each card had ten black smudges on it, one for each finger of some person far away. The smudges were made with ink. And the ink got everywhere.
"Ruksana!" her mother would call. "Why is there a thumb on the roti?"
There was. A small black whirl, right in the middle of the roti, like a tiny storm.
"It's mine," Ruksana said proudly. "I can tell."
"You can tell because there is ink on your thumb," said her mother. "Go and wash. With soap, not just water."

Ruksana went to the tap in the courtyard. She rubbed the soap until it foamed grey. The water alone had only made the ink shine. The soap lifted it. She held her thumb up to the evening light. Under the last grey streak, she could see fine lines on her skin, curving round and round like water going down a drain.

Every night Azizul Chacha sat at the low table with his cards and a lamp. He was a police sub-inspector. But he was also, everyone said, very good at numbers. His boss at the police office was an Englishman called Mr Henry. Mr Henry wanted to catch thieves by their fingerprints. A thief might change his name, or grow a beard. But he could not change the lines on his fingers.

"There is one problem," Chacha told Ruksana one night. He rubbed his eyes. "We have thousands of cards. Soon we will have lakhs. When a man is caught, we take his prints. Then we must find out if his card is already in our cupboards. How do we find one card among a lakh? A clerk would be looking until he was an old man."

Ruksana looked at the cards spread out under the lamp. Some fingers had whirls, like her right thumb. Some had loops that came in from one side, curved round like a hairpin, and went back out the same side. A few had plain little hills, rising and falling, like the arch of a bridge.
"Chacha," she said, "why do we have lines on our fingers at all?"
He smiled. "Feel this," he said. He put a single grain of rice on the table. "Shut your eyes. Find it with your finger."
She found it at once. She could feel it roll.
"Now find it with your elbow."
She could not. She giggled and pressed her elbow all over the table, and the grain stayed hidden.

"Your fingertips are your best feelers," said Chacha. "Maybe the lines help them feel, and help you hold things. Nobody knows for sure. What I do know is this. Along each line are tiny holes, too small to see. A little sweat comes out of them. Your fingers pick up a little oil from your face and hair too. So whenever you touch something, you leave your pattern behind, even without ink. You have been leaving yourself all over this house since you were born."
Ruksana looked around the room. The door. The water pot. Her slate. Her baby brother Faiz's cheek. She had touched them all. She was everywhere.

That night she could not sleep. She lay on her mat and thought about whirls, loops and hills. In the morning she made a game. She drew a big square on her slate and split it in two. On the left she wrote 'whirl'. On the right she wrote 'no whirl'. Then she went round the whole family, looking at right thumbs.

Her mother had a whirl. Her father had a loop. Faiz had a loop, though he tried to eat the slate. Old Nani's fingertips were so worn from forty years of grinding spices on the stone that Ruksana could hardly see the lines at all.
"They come back a little," said Nani, "when I rest my hands for a while." She laughed. "Even my skin knows when to take a holiday."
Ruksana showed her uncle the slate that evening. "I only asked one question," she said. "Whirl or no whirl? And it split everyone into two piles."
Azizul Chacha did not say anything for a long time. He looked at the slate. Then he looked at his own ten fingers, spread on the table.

"One question splits the cards into two piles," he said slowly. "But a person has ten fingers. Ask the same question for each finger. Whirl or no whirl, finger by finger. Then two piles become four. Four become eight. Eight become sixteen." He was already writing numbers down the side of a card. "Ten fingers. One thousand and twenty-four boxes. Not one great heap, but a thousand small ones. And each box has a number, worked out from the fingers themselves."
He looked up. His eyes were shining like a boy's.
"Did I help?" asked Ruksana.
"You asked a good question," he said. "Now I have to do a great deal of very boring arithmetic."

He did. For months he worked on it. He found ways to split the big boxes into smaller ones, by counting ridges and noticing tiny shapes. He worked with another clever man in the office, Hem Chandra Bose. In 1897, the government took up their system for all of India. A few years later, the police in London took it up too.
It was called the Henry System, after Mr Henry.
"Doesn't it make you cross?" Ruksana asked, when she heard the name. "It was your counting."

Azizul Chacha was quiet. Then he took her hand and turned it over, so her palm faced up. He pressed her fingertip, very gently, onto the clean glass of the lamp. When he lifted it, a faint whirl was there, made only of the sweat of her skin.
"You see that?" he said. "Nobody wrote your name on it. But anyone who looks carefully will know it is yours."

Ruksana grew up. She married, and moved to Dacca, and had children of her own. Their thumbs were often dirty too. Before every meal she sent them to the tap, with soap, and while they washed she made them hold their fingertips up to the light.
"Look," she would say. "That is you. You leave it on everything you touch. So be careful what you touch, and wash it off before you eat."

Many years later, the government gave her uncle a reward and an honour for his work, and Hem Chandra Bose too. By then, Ruksana had long known what she knew. On the lamp glass, on the water pot, on Faiz's cheek, she had seen it with her own eyes. The lines had been there before anyone gave them a name.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the fingertip is an external organ, and every part of it has a job. Its ridges help us feel, and perhaps grip. Tiny sweat pores along the ridges make us leave fingerprints on everything, which is why washing with soap matters before eating: soap lifts the oily layer that plain water cannot. The skin also wears and renews itself, as Nani's worn fingertips show. Underneath, the story asks who gets the credit for great work, through Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, whose names were left off the system they helped build.
ask: Why could Ruksana find the rice grain with her finger but not with her elbow?
How did Ruksana leave her pattern on things, even without ink?
Why did plain water not wash the ink off, but soap did?
Why do you think Nani's fingertip lines had almost worn away?
The system was named after Mr Henry. Who do you think should get the credit? Why?

games.title: Guard Match
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a matching card game about the outside of your body. Each body part has a guard that protects it, and a way we care for it. Players collect sets of three matching cards.

printables.title: 30 cards to cut out: 10 parts, 10 guards, 10 care cards
items: PART: Eyes
GUARD: Eyelashes, eyelids and tears
CARE: Never rub hard. Wash with clean water. Never look at the sun.
PART: Ears
GUARD: Earwax that moves out by itself
CARE: Wipe the outside only. Never poke anything in.
PART: Nose
GUARD: Nose hairs and sticky mucus
CARE: Blow gently into a handkerchief. Sneeze into your elbow.
PART: Teeth
GUARD: Hard enamel and spit
CARE: Brush twice a day, most of all at night.
PART: Skin
GUARD: A top layer of dead cells that renews itself
CARE: Bathe every day. Dry the folds. Cover cuts.
PART: Hair
GUARD: It keeps the head warm and shaded
CARE: Wash and comb. Don't share combs.
PART: Nails
GUARD: Hard keratin over the fingertips
CARE: Cut short and straight. Don't bite them.
PART: Hands
GUARD: Skin and a sense of touch that warns of heat
CARE: Wash with soap for 20 seconds.
PART: Feet
GUARD: Thick skin on the soles
CARE: Wash and dry between the toes. Wear chappals outside.
PART: Private parts
GUARD: Clothes, and the rule that your body belongs to you
CARE: Wash every day, wipe front to back, and tell a trusted adult if a touch feels wrong.

Sets of three

rules: Cut out the 30 cards. Shuffle them and lay them all face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over three cards and read them out loud.
If you have a PART, its GUARD and its CARE card, you win the set. Put it in that part's box on the mat.
If not, turn them back face down in the same places. Try to remember where they are.
When you win a set, explain how the guard protects the part. A good explanation wins a bonus point.
When all ten sets are won, the player with the most points wins.

options: dirt that we must dig out
a guard that traps dust and moves out by itself
a sign that you never bathe
check.why: Earwax traps dust and germs, then slowly moves out of the ear by itself. Picking 'dirt to dig out' is the most common idea, and it leads people to poke cotton buds in, which pushes wax deeper. Picking 'never bathe' mixes up wax with dirt. Even very clean people have earwax.

The top layer of skin is dead, so it can rub off without hurting. Thick soles protect feet. For private parts, a good answer is 'my body belongs to me, and I can tell a trusted adult'.

games.title: Who Am I? Body Riddles
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player reads a riddle in the voice of a body part. The others guess which part it is, and then act out how to care for it.

printables.title: 12 riddle cards
items: I am the biggest organ you have. I cover all of you. I flake off every day. Who am I? (Skin)
I am dead, but I keep growing. A haircut never hurts me. Who am I? (Hair)
I am hard and I grow about 3 millimetres a month. Germs love to hide under me. Who am I? (Nails)
I shut in a flash when something comes near. I spread tears over the eye. Who am I? (Eyelid)
I am sticky and yellow-brown. People think I am dirt, but I am a guard. Who am I? (Earwax)
I am a thin skin deep in your ear. I shake when sound arrives. Who am I? (Eardrum)
I warm the air, wet it and catch the dust in it. I also smell your dinner. Who am I? (Nose)
I am the hardest thing in your body, but germs that feed on sugar make acid that eats me. Who am I? (Enamel)
I can turn and touch every finger. Without me, holding a pencil is very hard. Who am I? (Thumb)
I carry all your weight. My middle curves up like a spring. Who am I? (Foot)
I am made of tiny ridges, and nobody else in the world has me. Who am I? (Fingerprint)
I am covered by your underwear. I am private. I belong to you. Who am I? (Private parts)

rules: Shuffle the riddle cards. One player is the reader.
The reader reads a riddle in the voice of the body part, without saying the answer in brackets.
The first to guess right gets the card.
Then everyone acts out one way to care for that part, for a token.
Swap readers each turn. The player with the most cards and tokens wins.

check.q: Game moment: 'I am dead, but I keep growing. A haircut never hurts me.' Who am I?
check.why: The hair you can see is made of dead cells, so cutting it does not hurt. It keeps growing because living cells at the root push it out. Skin is mostly alive underneath, and you can feel it. The eardrum is a living skin that shakes with sound.

flow.parent: If a child guesses 'nails' for the hair riddle, that is a good thought. Nails are also dead and growing. Ask what clue tells them apart: the haircut.

flow.kid: Make up your own riddle about a body part. Can the others guess?
