items.p: Which of these is an external organ?
items.why: Skin is on the outside, where we can see it. It is the biggest organ of the body. Picking heart, stomach or lungs shows you know they are organs, but they are inside the body, so they are internal organs.

items.p: The biggest organ of the body is the ____.
items.why: Skin covers the whole body. Spread out, a grown-up's skin would cover about one door.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each external organ has its own job. Some have more than one: the nose breathes and smells.

items.p: What do eyelashes do?
opts: Catch dust before it gets into the eye
Nothing, they are only for looks
items.why: Eyelashes catch dust and tiny bits in the air. Picking 'only for looks' is a common idea. Lashes do look nice, but they are also guards.

items.p: What is the best way to look after your ears?
opts: Clean inside with a cotton bud every day
Wipe the outside with a cloth, and never poke anything in
Put oil in them every week
Scratch inside with a hairpin when they itch
items.why: Ears clean themselves. Wax moves out by itself. Cotton buds, oil and hairpins can push wax deeper or hurt the eardrum. Picking the cotton bud is the most common mistake, because many people do it.

items.p: Earwax is a guard that traps dust and germs.
items.why: True. Wax traps dust and tiny germs and slowly moves out of the ear by itself.

items.p: When is the most important time to brush your teeth?
items.why: At night your mouth makes less spit, and spit protects teeth. So germs have all night to make acid. Brushing in the morning and at night is best. Picking 'when they look yellow' waits until damage has started.

items.p: Children have ____ milk teeth.
items.why: Children have 20 milk teeth. They fall out from about age 6, and bigger teeth grow in. A grown-up usually has 32.

items.p: Why do we wash hands with soap, not just water?
opts: Soap grabs the oil that germs stick to, so water can wash it away
Soap kills all germs instantly, even without rubbing
items.why: Germs stick in the thin layer of oil and grease on hands. Water slides over oil. Soap grabs oil, so water can carry it away. Picking 'kills instantly' misses that rubbing for 20 seconds matters: the rubbing and rinsing do much of the work.

items.p: Sort these into GOOD CARE and NOT GOOD CARE.
items: cutting nails short and straight
Good care
biting nails
Not good care
sneezing into your elbow
Good care
rubbing your eyes hard
Not good care
wearing chappals outside
Good care
sharing a comb with a friend
Not good care
items.a: see items
items.why: Good care helps each part's guards and keeps germs from spreading. Biting nails, rubbing eyes hard and sharing combs spread germs or hurt the body.

items.p: Cutting your hair hurts, because hair is alive.
items.why: False. The hair you can see is made of dead cells. Only the root under the skin is alive. That is why a haircut does not hurt.

items.p: What are private parts?
opts: The parts of the body covered by underwear
Any part of the body that is dirty
items.why: Private parts are the parts covered by underwear. Boys have a penis, girls have a vulva, and everyone has a bottom. We wash them every day. Picking 'dirty' is a common idea, but private parts are not dirty. They are private.

items.p: Someone touches your private parts and says it is a secret. What do you do?
opts: Say no, get away and tell a trusted grown-up
items.why: Secrets about touching should never be kept. It is never the child's fault. Say no, get away and tell a trusted grown-up. If they do not listen, tell another one.

items.p: Label the parts on the picture of a face: eyebrow, eyelashes, eyelid, nose, lips, ear.
items.a: Eyebrow above the eye, eyelashes on the edge of the eyelid, eyelid over the eye, nose in the middle, lips around the mouth, ear on the side of the head.
items.why: Naming each part helps you remember its job.
items.art: A simple outline of a child's face, front view, with empty label lines pointing to an eyebrow, eyelashes, an eyelid, the nose, the lips and one ear.

items.p: Draw your hand. Mark the places people most often forget when washing.
items.a: Thumbs, fingertips and nails, between the fingers, and the backs of the hands.
items.why: In the oily hands activity, the powder often stays on the thumbs, fingertips and backs of hands. Those are the places to rub carefully.

items.p: Name one guard of the nose and say how it helps.
items.a: Nose hairs catch dust as air comes in. Or: sticky mucus traps dust and germs, and I blow it out.
items.why: The nose's guards stop dust and germs getting deep inside you.

items.p: Why doesn't cutting a nail hurt?
opts: The part we cut is dead. Only the root under the skin is alive.
items.why: Nails are made of dead cells full of keratin. Living cells at the root push them out. Picking 'bone' mixes nails up with the skeleton. Nails are made of keratin, like hair and horns.

items.p: In the sticky tape test, white flakes stuck to the tape. What were they?
items.why: The top of the skin is dead cells that flake off as new cells grow underneath. Picking 'germs' is a good thought, but germs are far too small to see without a microscope.

items.p: Your outer skin is replaced by new skin about every month or two.
items.why: True. New cells grow underneath and push up. Old cells flake off. This is why scrapes heal and sunburn peels.

items.p: In the bread test, which slice usually grows the most spots?
opts: The slice touched with soap-washed hands
The slice touched with dirty hands
items.why: Dirty hands carry many germs and mould spores. On damp bread, each one grows into a spot. Picking 'all the same' would be true only if hands carried nothing.

items.p: Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month. About how long will they grow in 4 months?
items.why: 3 mm each month, for 4 months, is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 mm. Picking 30 mm mixes up millimetres and centimetres. 30 mm is 3 cm, far too much.

items.p: Match each guard to the part it protects.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each external organ has its own guard. Many guards, like wax and mucus, look like dirt but keep us safe.

items.p: Shaving hair makes it grow back thicker.
items.why: False. Cutting removes only the dead part. The root does not change. Mildred Trotter, an American scientist, tested this in 1928, and the hair grew back the same.

items.p: Why do ear doctors say no to cotton buds?
opts: Cotton buds are too soft to clean
They push wax deeper and can hurt the eardrum
items.why: Wax moves out by itself. A cotton bud often pushes it back in, and a hard poke can tear the eardrum. Picking 'too soft to clean' still imagines ears need digging out. They don't.

items.p: Why should you sneeze into your elbow, not your hand?
opts: Hands touch everything, so germs on them spread to others
items.why: Your hands touch door handles, food and people. Germs sneezed onto them spread quickly. Your elbow touches far less. Picking 'elbows are cleaner' is close, but the point is what each part touches next.

items.p: Using the correct names for private parts, like penis and vulva, is rude.
items.why: False. They are correct body words, like elbow or knee. Knowing them helps a child tell a doctor or trusted grown-up clearly if something is wrong.

items.p: In the egg test, the plain egg in vinegar bubbled and its shell went rough. What does this tell you about teeth?
items.a: Acid eats hard shells. Mouth germs make acid from sugar, so acid can eat tooth enamel too. Toothpaste helps protect it, so I should brush.
items.why: Eggshell and enamel are different minerals, but both are hard, both are made with calcium, and acid can dissolve both.

items.p: Why do you think germs can hide under long nails?
items.a: Long nails leave a gap where dirt collects, and soap and water can't reach in well. So germs stay there and get into food.
items.why: Short nails leave less space for dirt and germs.

items.p: Put the handwashing steps in order.
items: Wet your hands
Put on soap
Rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and nails for 20 seconds
Rinse with water
Dry on a clean towel
items.a: order shown
items.why: Wet, soap, rub for 20 seconds, rinse, dry. Most of the cleaning happens while rubbing.

items.p: Draw a cut-away of an ear. Show the funnel, the ear canal, the wax and the eardrum. Draw an arrow for which way the wax moves.
items.a: Funnel on the outside, a tube going in, wax in the tube, the eardrum at the end, an arrow pointing outwards.
items.why: Wax moves outwards, helped by the jaw moving. That is why ears mostly clean themselves.

items.p: Name your five trusted adults, or three if you can't think of five. Why did you choose each one?
items.a: Any real people the child knows and sees often, with a reason, such as 'Amma, because she always listens'.
items.why: Children need more than one trusted adult, in case one does not listen.

items.p: Hair and nails are dead, but they are part of you. Are they alive? Explain your answer.
items.a: A thoughtful answer, for example: the part I see is dead, because it has no nerves. But it was made by living cells, and it is still growing out from a living root. So it is part of a living body, even if it is not alive itself.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The line between living and non-living is not always clear.

items.p: Fingerprints form before birth. Identical twins have the same genes. Why do twins still have different fingerprints?
opts: Their fingerprints form in slightly different ways in the womb, with tiny differences in how each one grows and touches
Twins have different genes after all
One twin always has whorls and the other loops
items.why: Genes give the general pattern, but small differences in the womb, such as each baby's position and how its fingers grow, shape the exact ridges. Picking 'change every year' is wrong. Your fingerprints keep their shape all your life.

items.p: Scientists are completely sure what fingertip ridges are for.
items.why: False. Some think they help grip on rough or wet things. Some tests show they help us feel fine textures. It is still argued about.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out if warm water washes oily hands cleaner than cold water. What would you keep the same? What would you change?
items.a: Change only the water: warm or cold. Keep the same oil and powder, the same soap, and the same 20 seconds of rubbing. Look at how much powder is left each time.
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes.

items.p: David Strachan noticed in 1989 that children with more older brothers and sisters got hay fever less often. What idea did this start?
opts: That meeting some germs early might help the body
That older children have cleaner hands
That hay fever is caused by brothers
items.why: This became the hygiene hypothesis. Later scientists like Graham Rook thought meeting harmless 'old friend' microbes matters most. Handwashing at the right times is still important.

items.p: Your outer skin replaces itself every month or two. Some of the dust in your house is your old skin. Where do you think you end and the world begins?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: I thought I ended at my skin. But my old skin flakes off and becomes dust, and I leave fingerprints on everything I touch. So it is hard to say exactly where I stop.
items.why: This is a big question with no single answer. Good answers use what you saw in the sticky tape test.

items.p: In the story, the fingerprint system was named after Mr Henry, though Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose did much of the work. Is that fair? What could be done about it?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer with a reason. For example: it is not fair, because they did the counting. We could tell their story, and call it the Henry-Haque-Bose system.
items.why: In science, the people who did the work are not always the ones who get the name.

items.p: A child says, 'Water alone is fine, because I can't see any dirt.' What would you tell them, using the bread test?
opts: Germs are too small to see. The water-only slice grew more spots than the soap slice.
They are right, if you can't see it, it's not there
Bread has nothing to do with hands
items.why: Germs and mould spores are far too small to see. In the bread test they showed up as spots after a few days. Picking 'if you can't see it, it's not there' is the very idea the bread test shows is wrong.

items.p: Why might a long time on screens make your eyes dry and tired? Use what you found in the blink counter.
items.a: When we stare at a screen we blink much less. Each blink spreads tears over the eye. Fewer blinks means drier eyes.
items.why: Blinking spreads tears, which keep the eye wet and clean.

items.p: Design a new guard for one body part. Label what it does.
items.a: Any creative design with a clear job. For example: ear flaps that close in loud places, like a hippo's ears closing under water.
items.why: Good designs copy what real guards do: trap, steer away, or shut.
items.art: An empty box with 'my new guard' written at the top.

items.p: In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors washing their hands saved many mothers' lives, and most doctors believed him at once.
items.why: False. He showed handwashing saved lives, but many doctors refused to believe him for years. They did not like being told their own hands carried disease.

items.p: Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi became two of India's first women doctors, in 1886. Why might it matter for patients to have doctors of different kinds?
items.a: For example: some patients feel safer with a doctor like them. In those days many women would not let a male doctor examine them, so they got no care. More kinds of doctors means more people get help.
items.why: Everyone deserves a doctor they feel safe with, and a trusted grown-up with them.

items.p: Which is the best reason to wear chappals outside, especially near drains or wet soil?
opts: Some tiny worms in damp soil can get in through bare skin
items.why: Hookworms live in damp, dirty soil and can get in through the skin of bare feet. Chappals also protect from glass and hot roads. Picking 'look nicer' misses the health reason.

items.p: Some old Indian books describe cleaning teeth with neem twigs. Toothpaste with fluoride is newer. How could you find out which cleans better?
items.a: A fair test: some people use twigs and some use fluoride toothpaste for weeks, with everything else the same, and a dentist counts holes and germs. Or test on eggshells in vinegar.
items.why: Scientists test old and new ways fairly, instead of trusting what is old or what is new.

items.p: Is your body yours, even when you are small? Explain why.
items.a: Yes. My body belongs to me at every age. Grown-ups help care for it, but nobody has the right to touch it in a way that feels wrong.
items.why: This is the heart of body safety. A child's body belongs to the child.

experiments.title: The Bread Test: what do unwashed hands leave behind?
experiments.question: Do washed hands leave fewer germs on bread than unwashed hands? Does soap make a difference?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which slice will grow the most spots: touched by dirty hands, by hands washed in water only, or by hands washed with soap? Which will grow the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use slices from the same loaf, touch each one in the same way for the same time, and keep all the bags in the same dark cupboard. Only the hands change. Keep one slice untouched, so you can see what bread does on its own.

materials.item: slices of plain bread from one packet, or pav from one batch
small clear zip bags or plastic bags with tight knots
a clean spoon or tongs to put the untouched slice in its bag
a hand lens if you have one

experiments.safety: Never open the bags once they are sealed. Mould spores can upset breathing. At the end, throw the bags away still sealed. Wash hands after handling the bags.

schedule.what: Touch the slices, seal and label the bags, and put them in a dark cupboard.
Look at the bags without opening them. Count any spots.
Count spots a last time, draw the slices, fill in the table, and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 2, 4 and 6. On day 6, draw each slice. Then draw a bar for each slice, as tall as its number of spots.
experiments.context: This is the bread test. Hands touch slices of bread, after different kinds of washing. The slices sit in sealed bags for a few days. Any germs left on them grow into spots you can see.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: spots on each slice on day 6
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four slices of bread on a plate, a child's dusty hand touching one slice all over.
setup.caption: 1. Rub dirty hands over slice 1. Wash with water and touch slice 2. Wash with soap and touch slice 3.

setup.art: A grown-up using a clean spoon to slide a fourth slice into a bag without touching it.
setup.caption: 2. Put slice 4 in its bag without touching it.

setup.art: Four sealed, labelled bags lying in a dark cupboard.
setup.caption: 3. Seal and label the bags. Keep them in a dark cupboard.

setup.art: Four sealed bags on day 6: one with many green and black spots, one with a few, two almost clean.
setup.caption: 4. Count the spots on days 2, 4 and 6. Never open the bags.

flow.do: 1. Line up four slices and four bags. 2. Label the bags: Dirty hands, Water only, Soap, Untouched. 3. Ask your child to guess which slice will grow most spots.
flow.say: Our hands touch everything, and they pick up tiny living things too small to see. Let's find out what they leave on food.
flow.kid: Label four bags. Dirty hands. Water only. Soap. Untouched. Which slice will grow the most spots? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bread test. Germs left on bread grow into spots you can see. You label four bags and make a guess.
flow.parent: Bread from a local bakery, or pav, grows mould faster than packet bread, which often has preservatives in it. Sprinkle 5 drops of water on every slice before it goes in its bag, because mould grows best on damp bread. Keep the bags somewhere warm and dark.

flow.do: 1. Your child plays outside or touches door handles, shoes and the floor for two minutes. 2. They rub one slice all over with those hands, and seal it in the Dirty hands bag.
flow.say: First, the dirty hands. Touch slice 1 all over, on both sides, then seal it in.
flow.kid: Touch door handles and your shoes. Then rub slice 1 all over. Seal it in its bag.
flow.parent: Help your child seal the bag well. Squeeze out most of the air first. Do not use hands that have a cut on them.

flow.do: 1. Your child rinses hands under water only, for 20 seconds, and shakes them dry. 2. They touch slice 2 the same way and seal it. 3. Now they wash with soap for 20 seconds, rinse and shake them dry again. 4. They touch slice 3 and seal it.
flow.say: Now water only. Then soap. Touch each slice exactly the same way, so it's fair.
flow.kid: Wash with water only. Touch slice 2. Seal it. Now wash with soap for 20 seconds. Touch slice 3. Seal it.

check.q: Why do we touch each slice in the same way, for the same time?
options: So the test is fair, and only the washing is different
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is how the hands were washed. If one slice was rubbed much more, we would not know whether the spots came from the hands or the rubbing. Picking 'bread is soft' or 'stays fresh' misses the point of a fair test.

flow.do: Use a clean spoon to slide slice 4 into its bag, without touching it. Seal it. Put all four bags in a dark cupboard.
flow.say: This last slice is untouched. It shows what bread does all by itself.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to slide slice 4 in with a spoon. Don't touch it. Put all bags in a dark cupboard.
flow.parent: The untouched slice is the 'control'. It may grow a spot or two from the air. That is useful too: it shows germs are everywhere, and hands add more.

flow.do: On days 2, 4 and 6, look at the bags without opening them. Count the spots on each slice. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Don't open the bags. Just look and count.
flow.kid: Look at the bags. Do not open them. Count the spots on each slice. Write the numbers down.
flow.wait: Look on day 2, day 4 and day 6.

check.q: On day 6, the slice touched by dirty hands has the most spots. What does that show?
options: Hands carry tiny living things we cannot see
check.why: All the slices came from the same loaf and the same kind of bag. The only difference was the hands. So the extra spots came from germs and mould spores on the hands. Picking 'older bread' misses that all slices were the same. Picking 'the bag' misses that all bags were the same too.

flow.parent: Spots often show first on day 3 or 4. In a cool room or with packet bread, it can take longer. If there are no spots by day 6, keep looking every two days until day 10. Results vary, so trust what you see, and talk about it if the slices look alike.

flow.do: Compare the slices. Which grew the most? The fewest? Did water alone work as well as soap?
flow.say: Was your guess right? What did soap do that water alone didn't?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Which slice is cleanest? Did soap beat water?
flow.think: Before which jobs in a day should you always wash with soap?
flow.parent: Plain water washes off some germs. But many stick in the thin layer of oil and grease on hands. Soap grabs the oil, so water can carry it, and the germs, away. Fuzzy mould spots are fungi, and the colours show different kinds. Small shiny spots may be bacteria.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things about the bread test. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: washing with soap takes away the most germs. What I saw: the dirty-hands slice had 11 spots, water only had 6, and soap had 2. Why: soap lifts the oily layer that germs stick to.
flow.context: This is the end of the bread test. Your child says what they found, using claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Sticky Tape Skin: are you falling off?
experiments.question: Is your skin always shedding tiny bits of itself?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will anything stick to the tape? Will the arm and the elbow give the same amount? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same length of tape and press for the same time on each place. Use dark paper for every strip, so the flakes show up the same.
results_table: How many flakes, roughly: none, a few, lots

materials.item: a sheet of black or dark blue paper
a hand lens if you have one

experiments.safety: Use gentle tape. Do not press on cuts, rashes or sore skin. Peel slowly.

schedule.what: Press tape on three places, stick the strips on dark paper, look closely and record.

experiments.record: Stick the three strips on the dark paper and label each one. Fill in the table. Draw what you see through the lens.
experiments.context: This is the sticky tape test. You press clear tape on your skin, peel it off and stick it on dark paper. Then you look closely at what came off.

setup.art: A strip of clear tape pressed on the inside of a child's forearm.
setup.caption: 1. Press clear tape firmly on your arm for 5 seconds.

setup.art: The tape being slowly peeled off the arm.
setup.caption: 2. Peel it off slowly.

setup.art: Three tape strips on black paper, with tiny white flakes, and a hand lens over one.
setup.caption: 3. Stick it on dark paper. Look with a lens.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess: will anything come off on the tape?
flow.say: Your skin looks smooth and whole. Let's see if any of it is coming off.
flow.kid: Will anything come off your skin onto tape? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sticky tape test. It shows whether your skin is shedding bits of itself.

flow.do: 1. Press a strip of tape on the inside of the forearm for 5 seconds. Peel it slowly and stick it on the dark paper. 2. Do the same on the elbow and the back of the hand. 3. Label each strip.
flow.say: Press, count to five, peel slowly, and stick it down.
flow.kid: Press tape on your arm. Count to five. Peel slowly. Stick it on dark paper. Now try your elbow and your hand.

flow.do: Look at the strips closely, with a hand lens if you have one. Count roughly how many flakes are on each.
flow.say: What do you see on the tape? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: Look closely. What are the tiny white flakes?

check.q: The tiny white flakes on the tape are…
options: dead skin cells that were ready to fall off
dust that was sitting on your skin
check.why: The top layer of skin is made of flat, dead cells. New cells grow underneath and push them up, and the old ones flake off. Picking 'dust' is a good thought, because some dust does sit on skin. But the flakes are flat and white, like skin, and they come off even after a bath. Picking 'pieces of tape' misses that clean tape on paper has no flakes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things about the sticky tape test. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my skin is always shedding. What I saw: tiny white flakes on every strip, and the most on my elbow. Why: the top layer is dead cells that flake off as new skin grows underneath.
flow.context: This is the end of the sticky tape test. Your child says what they found, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: The Egg That Brushed Its Teeth
experiments.question: Can toothpaste protect a hard shell from acid?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After a night in vinegar, which egg will have the softer, rougher shell: the plain one, or the one covered in toothpaste? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two eggs of the same kind, two same-sized glasses, and the same amount of vinegar. Only the toothpaste changes. Leave both for the same time.
results_table: Shell after one night: smooth or rough?
Shell after one night: hard or soft?

materials.item: toothpaste with fluoride (most toothpastes in India have it: check the tube)

experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the raw eggs. Wash hands after touching raw egg. Do not eat the eggs afterwards. Vinegar stings eyes, so keep it away from faces.

schedule.what: Cover one egg in toothpaste and leave it for an hour. Then put both eggs in vinegar and watch the bubbles.
Take the eggs out with a spoon, rinse them, feel the shells and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both eggs on day 2, and label which was smooth and which was rough.
experiments.context: This is the egg test. Eggshell is a hard mineral a little like tooth enamel. One egg is covered in toothpaste, one is not, and both sit in vinegar, which is an acid, like the acid mouth germs make.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands smearing white toothpaste all over a raw egg on a saucer.
setup.caption: 1. Cover one egg all over in toothpaste. Leave it for an hour.

setup.art: Two glasses of vinegar, each with an egg, one plain and one wiped of toothpaste, tiny bubbles rising from the plain one.
setup.caption: 2. Wipe it gently, then put both eggs in vinegar.

setup.art: Two rinsed eggs on a cloth the next day, a child's finger feeling one rough, chalky shell.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, rinse them and feel the shells.

flow.do: Show your child the two eggs. Tap them gently. Say that eggshell is a hard mineral, a little like tooth enamel.
flow.say: Your teeth have a hard coat called enamel. Mouth germs make acid from sugar, and acid eats enamel. Vinegar is an acid too. Let's see what it does to a hard shell.
flow.kid: Eggshell is hard, a bit like your teeth. Vinegar is an acid. What will it do?
flow.context: This is the first step of the egg test. It shows what acid does to a hard shell, and whether toothpaste protects it.

flow.do: Cover one egg completely in toothpaste and leave it on a saucer for one hour. Then wipe off most of the paste gently with a tissue.
flow.say: This egg is brushing its teeth. We give the toothpaste time to soak into the shell.
flow.kid: A grown-up covers one egg in toothpaste. Wait one hour. Then wipe it gently.

flow.do: Put each egg in its own glass. Pour vinegar over both until they are covered. Watch for one or two minutes.
flow.say: Look closely at the shells. What is coming off them?
flow.kid: Put both eggs in vinegar. Watch. What do you see on the shells?

check.q: Tiny bubbles come off the plain egg's shell. What is happening?
options: The acid is eating the shell and giving off a gas
check.why: Vinegar is an acid. It reacts with the chalky shell, dissolving it bit by bit and giving off a gas called carbon dioxide. That is the bubbles. Picking 'breathing' is a good thought, because an eggshell has tiny holes that let air through. But these bubbles are made by the acid. Picking 'boiling' misses that the vinegar is cold.

flow.parent: The toothpaste egg may bubble less, or start later. Results vary with the toothpaste. That is fine: talk about what you see.

flow.do: Next day, lift each egg out with a spoon and rinse it. Let your child feel both shells.
flow.say: Feel both shells. Which is rougher? Which is softer?
flow.kid: Lift out the eggs with a spoon. Rinse them. Feel both shells. Which is rough?
flow.wait: Leave both eggs in the vinegar overnight.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things about the egg test. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: toothpaste helps protect a shell from acid. What I saw: the plain egg bubbled a lot and its shell went rough, but the toothpaste egg stayed smoother. Why: the toothpaste left a thin coat on the shell that slowed the acid down. Fluoride in toothpaste helps tooth enamel stand up to acid in a similar way. If both eggs look the same, that is a real result too. Talk about why it might have happened.
flow.context: This is the end of the egg test. Your child says what they found, with claim, evidence and reasoning.

activities.title: Outside-Me Map

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or newspapers taped together, as long as your child

schedule.what: Draw round your child, label the external organs, and write one job for each.

activities.record: Keep the map on the wall. Through the unit, add one care rule next to each part.
activities.context: This is a drawing activity. You trace round your child on big paper, then label every part you can see from the outside, with its job.

setup.art: A child lying on big paper on the floor, arms a little apart, a parent drawing round them with a crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Lie on the paper. A grown-up draws round you.

setup.art: A child looking in a mirror at their ear and nose.
setup.caption: 2. Look in a mirror. Name every part you can see.

setup.art: The traced outline on a wall with labels and arrows: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin, hair, nails, hands, feet, private parts.
setup.caption: 3. Label each part and write its job.

flow.do: Your child lies on the paper with arms and legs a little apart. Draw round them with a crayon.
flow.say: Lie very still. I'm going to draw the outside of you.
flow.kid: Lie still on the paper. A grown-up draws round you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Outside-Me Map. You make a life-size outline of your child to label.

flow.do: Give your child a mirror. Ask them to name every part they can see on the outside of their body. Write each one on a label.
flow.say: What can you see from the outside? Look closely. Don't forget the small parts, like nails and eyebrows.
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Name every part you can see. Even tiny ones, like eyebrows.

ask.q: What do we call the parts we can see on the outside?

check.q: Which of these is an external organ?
check.why: Skin is on the outside, where you can see it, so it is an external organ. In fact, it is the biggest organ you have. The heart and lungs are inside the chest, so they are internal organs. Picking them is a good sign you know they are organs. Ask: can I see it in a mirror?

flow.parent: Expect skin, hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, teeth, tongue, hands, nails and feet. Name the private parts calmly too: 'the parts covered by your underwear'. Using the correct names, penis and vulva, is normal and helps children stay safe.

flow.do: Stick each label on the outline with an arrow. Next to each, your child writes or draws one job that part does.
flow.say: Every part has a job. What does your nose do? What do your nails do?
flow.kid: Stick on each label. Next to it, write or draw its job.
flow.parent: Simple jobs are fine: eyes see, ears hear, nose breathes and smells, skin covers and feels, nails protect fingertips, feet carry us. Children often forget that skin is an organ. Ask, 'What covers all of you?'

flow.do: Put the map on the wall. Say you will add a care rule next to each part as the unit goes on.
flow.say: This map will grow. Each time we learn how to care for a part, we'll add it.
flow.kid: Put your map on the wall. You will add care rules to it soon.
flow.think: Which part do you think has the most jobs?

activities.title: Fingerprint Detective

materials.item: a soft pencil (2B or darker) and a scrap of paper
a hand lens if you have one
an ink pad, if you have one (the pencil works just as well)

activities.safety: Wash hands with soap afterwards, because graphite and ink are messy.

schedule.what: Take thumbprints, compare your own two thumbs, then take the family's prints, sort them into loops, whorls and arches, and count each kind.

activities.record: Stick your two thumbprints side by side and circle a ridge fork on each. Stick each person's thumbprint on the paper with their name. Make a tally of loops, whorls and arches.
activities.context: This is a fingerprint activity. You take prints with pencil and tape, compare your own two thumbs, and sort the family's prints into three kinds: loops, whorls and arches.

setup.art: A child rubbing a pencil hard on paper to make a dark patch, then rubbing a fingertip on it.
setup.caption: 1. Make a dark pencil patch. Rub your fingertip on it.

setup.art: Clear tape pressed on a grey fingertip, then stuck on white paper, showing a clear print.
setup.caption: 2. Press tape on the fingertip. Stick the tape on white paper.

setup.art: A left and a right thumbprint side by side on white paper under a hand lens, with a small Y-shaped ridge fork circled on one.
setup.caption: 3. Put your two thumbprints side by side. Look for a ridge that splits in two.

setup.art: Three big prints side by side, labelled loop, whorl and arch.
setup.caption: 4. Sort each print: loop, whorl or arch.

flow.do: 1. Scribble hard with a soft pencil to make a dark patch. 2. Rub your child's thumb on it until it is grey. 3. Press clear tape on the thumb, peel it, and stick it on white paper.
flow.say: Fingertips have tiny ridges. Let's catch yours on tape.
flow.kid: Rub your thumb on the pencil patch. Press tape on it. Peel it off. Stick it on white paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fingerprint Detective. You take a thumbprint using pencil and sticky tape.

flow.do: Look at the print with a hand lens. Show the three kinds: a loop comes in from one side and goes back out the same side. A whorl goes round and round. An arch rises like a small hill.
flow.say: Which kind is yours: a loop, a whorl or an arch?
flow.kid: Look closely. Is yours a loop, a whorl or an arch?

check.q: A print has lines that go round and round, like water down a drain. What kind is it?
check.why: A whorl goes round and round in circles or a spiral. A loop curves round like a hairpin and goes back out the side it came in. An arch rises and falls like a hill. Picking 'loop' is a near miss, because loops also curve. Check whether the lines go all the way round.

flow.do: 1. Make a print of your child's left thumb the same way, and stick it next to the right one. 2. Before looking closely, ask your child whether the two prints will match, and why. 3. Use a hand lens to look at the right print. Find a place where a ridge splits in two, like the letter Y, or where a ridge stops. Circle it. 4. Look at the same place on the left print.
flow.say: Your two thumbs grew from the same genes. Do you think their prints will match? Why do you think so? Now find a ridge that splits in two, like a Y. Is there one in the same place on your other thumb?
flow.kid: Print your left thumb too. Put it next to the right one. Will they match? Find a ridge that splits like a Y. Circle it. Is there one in the same place on the other print?
flow.parent: Genes are the instructions inside your cells that guide how your body grows. The two prints often look like mirror images, and they may be the same kind, such as two whorls. But the small forks and ends will not be in the same places. If a print is smudged, make a darker pencil patch and try again.

check.q: Your two thumbs grew from the same genes. What did you find when you compared their prints closely?
options: The forks and ends of the ridges were in different places
check.why: Every finger has its own print, even though the cells in both thumbs carry the same genes. The ridges formed before you were born, and tiny differences in how each fingertip grew set the details. If your prints looked the same at first, look again at the small forks. They will not match. 'No ridges' only happens when a print is smudged.

flow.do: Take the right thumbprint of everyone at home. Label each with the person's name. Sort them into loops, whorls and arches. Make a tally.
flow.say: Is anyone's print the same as yours? Even people in the same family?
flow.kid: Take everyone's thumbprint. Write their names. Sort them. Count each kind.
flow.parent: Loops are the most common kind, then whorls. Arches are rare. Family members often have similar kinds, but never the same exact print.

flow.do: Wash hands with soap. Look at how well soap removes the grey graphite compared with water alone.
flow.say: Pencil and oil stick to skin. Watch what soap does.
flow.kid: Wash with soap. Watch the grey come off.
flow.think: What other animals do you think have fingerprints?
flow.parent: Koalas, chimpanzees and gorillas have fingerprints too.

activities.title: Oily Hands: water or soap?

materials.item: a few drops of coconut or cooking oil
a pinch of haldi (turmeric) powder, or a pinch of glitter
a clock or a song to time 20 seconds

activities.safety: Haldi can stain skin and nails yellow for a few hours. That's harmless. If you use glitter, keep it away from eyes.

schedule.what: Coat hands in oil and 'germs', try washing with water, then with soap, and learn the steps of handwashing.

activities.record: Draw your hands after water only and after soap. Then draw the six steps of handwashing.
activities.context: This is a handwashing activity. Haldi powder or glitter stands in for germs on oily hands. You see what water alone does, then what soap does.

setup.art: A child's hands rubbed with oil and sprinkled with yellow haldi powder.
setup.caption: 1. Rub a few drops of oil on your hands. Sprinkle on haldi or glitter.

setup.art: Hands in a bowl of plain water, the yellow powder still stuck on.
setup.caption: 2. Wash with water only. Look at your hands.

setup.art: Soapy hands rubbing between the fingers, the yellow powder coming away.
setup.caption: 3. Now wash with soap for 20 seconds. Look again.

flow.do: Rub a few drops of oil over your child's hands. Sprinkle on a pinch of haldi or glitter. Say the powder is pretend germs.
flow.say: Hands pick up a thin layer of oil from food, from your face and from things you touch. Germs stick in that oil. Let's pretend this powder is germs.
flow.kid: Rub oil on your hands. Sprinkle on the powder. Pretend it is germs.
flow.context: This is the first step of the oily hands activity. Glitter stands in for germs on oily skin.

flow.do: Your child washes in plain water for 20 seconds, then shakes their hands and looks.
flow.say: Did water alone get the germs off?
flow.kid: Wash with water only for 20 seconds. Look. Is the powder gone?

check.q: After water only, most of the powder is still stuck on. Why?
options: Water and oil don't mix, so water slides over the oil
We didn't use hot enough water
The powder can never come off
check.why: Oil and water don't mix. Water runs over oily skin without lifting the oil, so anything stuck in the oil stays put. Picking 'hot water' is a common idea. Warm water feels nicer, but soap matters much more than heat. Picking 'can never come off' is about to be proved wrong.

flow.do: Now wash with soap, rubbing for 20 seconds. Teach the six steps. Rub the palms, then the backs of the hands, then between the fingers. Then rub the backs of the fingers, the thumbs, and the fingertips and nails. Then rinse.
flow.say: Soap grabs oil with one end and water with the other. So water can carry the oil, and the germs, away. Let's count 20 seconds, or sing Happy Birthday twice.
flow.kid: Now use soap. Rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and nails. Sing Happy Birthday twice. Rinse.
flow.parent: Children often wash only their palms. The thumbs, fingertips and backs of the hands are the places most often missed. Watch where the powder stays. Haldi may leave a faint yellow tint even after soap. That is dye soaked into the skin, so look for the grains of powder instead.

flow.do: Look at the hands. Where is the powder still stuck? Talk about when to wash with soap. Wash before eating, after the toilet, after playing outside and after touching animals. Wash after sneezing into your hands too.
flow.say: When are the most important times to wash with soap?
flow.kid: Where is the powder still stuck? When must you wash with soap? Say four times.

ask.q: When should we always wash hands with soap?

flow.think: Why do you think thumbs and fingertips are the most often missed?

activities.title: My Trusted Hand
activities.safety: Keep the tone warm and ordinary, like teaching road safety. If your child tells you something worrying, stay calm, thank them, and get help. In India, you can call the Childline number 1098, or 112.

schedule.what: Learn the body safety rules, trace a hand and name five trusted adults, and practise saying No.

activities.record: Stick the trusted hand on the wall next to the Outside-Me Map.
activities.context: This is a body safety activity. Your child learns that their body belongs to them, and names five grown-ups they can always tell.

setup.art: A child tracing round their own hand on paper with a crayon.
setup.caption: 1. Trace round your hand.

setup.art: The traced hand with a small drawing of a grown-up's face on each finger and 'My body belongs to me' on the palm.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a trusted grown-up on each finger.

setup.art: A child standing tall, palm held out, saying 'No!' firmly, with a parent smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Practise saying No, firmly and loudly.

flow.do: Say the rules calmly and simply. Use the correct names: penis, vulva and bottom.
flow.say: Your private parts are the parts covered by your underwear. They are private. Your body belongs to you. Nobody should touch your private parts, or ask to see them, or ask you to touch theirs. The only times are when a parent is helping you keep clean, or a doctor is checking you with me there. If any touch feels wrong or confusing, it is never your fault. Say no, get away and tell me or another trusted grown-up.
flow.kid: Your body belongs to you. Private parts are private. If a touch feels wrong, say no. Get away. Tell a trusted grown-up.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Trusted Hand. It is about keeping your body safe.
flow.parent: Children learn this best when it is said like any other safety rule, without fear. You may also say: some people may try to trick a child into a secret. Good secrets, like a birthday surprise, are fun and end soon. Secrets about touching are never kept.

flow.do: Ask your child the question below. Listen to their answer and gently fill gaps.
flow.say: What would you do if someone said, 'This touch is our secret'?
flow.kid: Someone says, 'This touch is our secret.' What do you do?

ask.q: What would you do if someone said a touch was a secret?

check.q: Someone you know asks you to keep a secret about touching. What should you do?
options: Keep the secret, because they are a grown-up
Tell a trusted grown-up, even if you promised
Feel bad, because it must be your fault
check.why: Secrets about touching should never be kept, even if you promised and even if the person is someone you know. Telling a trusted grown-up is always right, and it is never your fault. Picking 'they are a grown-up' is a common idea, because children are taught to obey. But your body belongs to you. Picking 'my fault' is what tricksters want children to feel. It is never true.

flow.do: Your child traces their hand. On each finger, they draw or write one grown-up they trust and could tell anything. On the palm, they write: My body belongs to me.
flow.say: Who are five grown-ups you could tell anything to? Would they listen? Could you reach them?
flow.kid: Trace your hand. On each finger, draw a grown-up you trust. On the palm, write: My body belongs to me.
flow.parent: Help your child choose people they actually see often. If one does not listen, the child should tell the next one.

flow.do: Practise together: stand tall, hold out a palm and say 'No!' loudly. Then practise walking away and finding a grown-up.
flow.say: Say it like you mean it. Stand tall. 'No!'
flow.kid: Stand tall. Hold up your hand. Say No, loudly. Then walk away and find a grown-up.
flow.parent: Children often find this funny. That is fine. Laughing helps it stick.

activities.title: Blink Counter and the Eyebrow Test

materials.item: a cup of water and a spoon

activities.safety: Use only clean water, a few drops at a time, on the forehead, never in the eyes.

schedule.what: Count blinks for one minute, then see how eyebrows send drips aside.

activities.record: Write how many times you blinked in one minute. Draw where the water drops ran.
activities.context: This is an activity about the guards of the eyes. You count how often a person blinks, and see what eyebrows do with water running down the forehead.

setup.art: A child watching a parent's eyes and making tally marks while a timer runs.
setup.caption: 1. Count a grown-up's blinks for one minute.

setup.art: A grown-up dripping a few drops of water from a spoon on a child's forehead above one eyebrow, the child's eyes closed, a towel ready.
setup.caption: 2. Drip a few drops of water above your eyebrow.

setup.art: Water drops running round the curve of an eyebrow and down the side of the face, away from the eye.
setup.caption: 3. Watch where the water runs.

flow.do: Your child watches your eyes for one minute while you chat normally, and makes a tally mark at every blink. Swap.
flow.say: Every blink spreads tears over your eyes and wipes away dust. Count how many times I blink in one minute.
flow.kid: Watch a grown-up's eyes for one minute. Make a mark every time they blink.
flow.context: This is the first step of the blink counter. You count how often a person blinks.
flow.parent: Grown-ups usually blink about 15 to 20 times a minute when talking. Children often blink less. When reading or looking at a screen, people blink much less, which is why eyes get dry.

flow.do: Your child closes their eyes and tips their head back a little. Drip a few drops of water on the forehead just above one eyebrow. Watch where it runs.
flow.say: Where does the water go when it reaches the eyebrow?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. A grown-up drips water above your eyebrow. Where does it run?

check.q: The water runs round the eyebrow and down the side of the face. What is the eyebrow's job?
options: To send sweat and rain away from the eyes
To make the face look nice, and nothing more
check.why: The arch shape and the hairs of the eyebrow steer drips from the forehead around the eye, so sweat and rain don't sting the eyes. Picking 'to look nice' is very common. Eyebrows also show feelings, but they have a guard's job too.

flow.do: Talk about the other eye guards: eyelashes, eyelids and tears. Add 'eye care' to the Outside-Me Map.
flow.say: Name all the guards of your eyes. Which one did you see working today?
flow.kid: Name your eye's guards. Lashes, lids, tears, brows. Add them to your map.
flow.think: Why do people blink less when they stare at a screen?

activities.title: The Wax Escalator (act it out)

materials.item: a long scarf or dupatta for the ear canal
a few small balls of paper as dust

activities.safety: Act it out only. Nothing goes into anyone's ear.

schedule.what: Act out how earwax traps dust and moves out of the ear.

activities.record: Draw a cut-away of the ear with the wax moving outwards, and write 'never poke in' next to it.
activities.context: This is a play-acting activity. You act out how earwax traps dust inside the ear and slowly carries it out.

setup.art: A long dupatta laid on the floor like a tunnel, with a cushion at the far end labelled 'eardrum'.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a dupatta on the floor as the ear canal. A cushion is the eardrum.

setup.art: A child crouched on the dupatta holding paper balls, shuffling slowly towards the open end while another child chews and talks.
setup.caption: 2. One child is the wax. They catch the dust and shuffle out as the 'jaw' chews.

flow.do: Lay the dupatta on the floor as the ear canal. Put a cushion at one end as the eardrum. Throw paper balls in as dust.
flow.say: This is the inside of an ear. Dust is blowing in. Who will stop it reaching the eardrum?
flow.kid: The dupatta is your ear tube. The cushion is your eardrum. Paper balls are dust blowing in.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wax Escalator, an act-it-out about how earwax cleans the ear.

flow.do: Your child plays the wax. They catch the paper balls before they reach the cushion. Each time you chew or talk loudly, they shuffle one step out of the ear, carrying the dust.
flow.say: Every time I chew or talk, my jaw moves, and the wax moves out a little.
flow.kid: You are the wax. Catch the dust. Each time the grown-up chews, shuffle one step out.

check.q: In the play, a cotton bud comes in. What does it do to the wax?
options: Pushes it back towards the eardrum
Helps it out faster every time
check.why: A cotton bud is wider than the wax's path out, so it often pushes wax deeper, towards the eardrum, and it can scratch or tear it. Picking 'helps it out' is what most people believe, because some wax comes out on the bud. But more is pushed in.

flow.do: Swap roles. Then talk: what should we do with ears? Add the ear care rule to the Outside-Me Map.
flow.say: So what's our ear rule?
flow.kid: Swap roles. Then say the ear rule: wipe the outside, never poke in.
flow.think: If wax is a guard, why does a doctor sometimes take some out?
flow.parent: Sometimes wax gets stuck and blocks hearing. Then a doctor removes it safely. Don't use oil, sticks or ear candles at home unless a doctor tells you to.

projects.title: How Fast Do I Grow? The Nail Tracker

materials.item: a non-toxic marker or a bit of nail paint

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts nails. Do not cut too short, and keep the edges straight.

schedule.what: Cut the thumbnails. Make a tiny mark on the nail just above the skin. Measure the gap between the mark and the skin: zero.
Measure the gap between the skin and the mark. Remark the nail if it has faded.
Measure again. Work out how far the nail grew in two weeks, and guess how far in a month and in a year.

projects.record: A table of the date and the gap in millimetres for your thumbnail and a grown-up's. Then a bar chart.
projects.context: This is a two-week project. You mark a thumbnail and measure how far the mark moves as the nail grows.

setup.art: A tiny dot of nail paint on a child's thumbnail just above the skin.
setup.caption: 1. Make a tiny mark on the nail, just above the skin.

setup.art: A ruler held next to a thumb, the mark a little way up the nail.
setup.caption: 2. Each week, measure the gap from the skin to the mark.

setup.art: A small bar chart with two bars: child and grown-up.
setup.caption: 3. Compare your nail with a grown-up's.

flow.do: Cut both thumbnails. Make a tiny mark on the nail, right at the edge of the skin. Do the same on a grown-up's thumbnail. Write the date.
flow.say: Nails grow from a living root under the skin. The mark will ride up as the nail grows, like a passenger on a slow train.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts your nails. Make a tiny mark at the bottom of your thumbnail. Do one on a grown-up too.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nail Tracker. You mark a thumbnail so you can measure how fast it grows.

flow.do: On day 8, measure the gap from the skin to the mark, in millimetres. Write it down. Remark if it has faded.
flow.say: How far has the mark moved in one week?
flow.kid: Measure from your skin to the mark. Write the number in millimetres.

flow.do: On day 15, measure again for both people. Make a bar chart.
flow.say: Whose nail grew faster? Grown-ups or children?
flow.kid: Measure again. Draw a bar for you and one for the grown-up.

check.q: Why doesn't cutting your nail hurt, even though it grows?
options: The part you cut is dead. Only the root under the skin is alive.
Nails have no cells at all
check.why: The nail you see is made of dead cells packed with keratin. Living cells at the root, under the skin, make new nail and push it out. The cut part has no nerves, so cutting it does not hurt. Picking 'no cells at all' is close, but nails are made of cells, just dead ones. Picking 'quickly' misses why: speed does not stop pain.

flow.parent: Children's nails usually grow a little faster than older grown-ups'. Expect about 1 to 2 millimetres in two weeks. Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month on average.

flow.do: Talk about what you found and what it means for care.
flow.say: If nails grow about 3 millimetres a month, how often should we cut them?
flow.kid: How often should you cut your nails? Why do germs like long nails?
flow.think: Your nail is made of dead cells, but it is part of you. Is it alive or not?

challenges.title: Build a Tippy Tap
challenges.problem: In many places there is no tap or sink. People still need to wash their hands with soap, without touching a dirty handle. Build a handwashing station from a plastic bottle, which you work with your foot.
constraints: Your hands must not touch the bottle to tip it.
It must use very little water.
The soap must stay clean and close by.
materials: a 1 or 2 litre plastic bottle with its cap
two sticks, or a chair back to hang it from
a bar of soap with a hole in it, or soap in an old sock
a thick nail or skewer for a grown-up to make a hole
general: The tippy tap: a bottle hung on a stick, tied to a foot pedal stick with string. Pressing the pedal tips the bottle and pours a thin stream.
A pot with a small tap fitted near the bottom.
A bucket and mug, poured by a friend.
creative: Hang the soap on a string, so it never sits in a dirty puddle.
Put stones under the tap, so the water soaks away and makes no mud for mosquitoes.
Make it at child height, with a picture of the six handwashing steps beside it.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design and label each part. Then build it with a grown-up, and test it: how many handwashes does one bottle give?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a handwashing station you can use without touching it with dirty hands. It is called a tippy tap.

setup.art: A grown-up making a small hole near the neck of a plastic bottle with a heated nail held by pliers.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a small hole near the bottle's neck.

setup.art: The bottle hanging by string from a horizontal stick between two upright sticks, with a string to a foot pedal stick on the ground.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the bottle and tie it to a foot pedal.

setup.art: A child pressing the pedal with a foot, the bottle tipping and pouring a thin stream on soapy hands.
setup.caption: 3. Press the pedal. Wash with soap.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the picture of the finished tippy tap.
flow.say: In many schools and villages, there is no sink. How could people wash hands without touching a dirty handle?
flow.kid: Many places have no sink. How could you wash without touching a dirty tap?
flow.context: This is the first step of the tippy tap challenge. You plan a handwashing station worked by your foot.

flow.do: Your child draws a design and labels the parts: the bottle, the stick, the string, the pedal and the soap.
flow.say: Draw your design first. Show where the water comes out.
flow.kid: Draw your design. Label the bottle, string, pedal and soap.

flow.do: A grown-up makes a small hole near the neck of the bottle. Fill it with water. Hang it, tie it to a pedal stick, and hang soap beside it.
flow.say: Now we build it. I'll make the hole, because it needs a hot or sharp tool.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the hole. You help hang the bottle and tie the pedal.

flow.do: Test it. Count how many handwashes one bottle gives.
flow.say: Does it work? What would you change?
flow.kid: Press the pedal and wash. How many washes from one bottle?

check.q: Why is the tippy tap worked with your foot?
options: So dirty hands don't touch it and spread germs to the next person
check.why: A tap handle touched by dirty hands passes germs to the next person who touches it. A foot pedal keeps hands off. Picking 'feet are stronger' misses that the bottle is light. Picking 'save soap' mixes it up with how much soap you use.

challenges.title: Eyebrows for a Robot
challenges.problem: A robot has two camera eyes on its face. When it works in the rain or gets hot, drips run down its forehead and blur the cameras. Design guards for its eyes, using what you learned from your own eyebrows and eyelashes.
constraints: The cameras must still see clearly in front.
It must work when drops come from above.
materials: a cardboard box or a plastic bottle for the robot's head
two bottle caps for camera eyes
paper, card, cotton wool, string, tape, an old toothbrush
a spoon and a cup of water for testing
general: A ridge above each eye, shaped like an eyebrow, to steer drips to the side.
A peak like a cap's brim.
A wiper, like a car's windscreen wiper.
creative: A row of bristles from an old toothbrush above each eye, like eyelashes.
A groove like a gutter along the forehead.
A slanted forehead, so drips run off to the sides.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design. Then build it on a box head and test it with drops of water from a spoon. Did the drips miss the eyes?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You protect a robot's camera eyes from drips, copying the way eyebrows and eyelashes protect your eyes.

setup.art: A cardboard box robot head with two bottle-cap eyes.
setup.caption: 1. Make a robot head with two bottle-cap eyes.

setup.art: Curved card strips taped above each bottle-cap eye like eyebrows.
setup.caption: 2. Build eyebrows or a brim above the eyes.

setup.art: Water dripping from a spoon onto the box forehead and running round the card brows, away from the eyes.
setup.caption: 3. Drip water on the forehead. Did it miss the eyes?

flow.do: Remind your child of the eyebrow test, or do it now. Look at eyebrows in the mirror: their shape and which way the hairs point.
flow.say: Your eyebrows curve and their hairs point sideways. Why would that help?
flow.kid: Look at your eyebrows in the mirror. Which way do the hairs point?
flow.context: This is the first step of the robot eyebrow challenge. You look at your own eyebrows to get ideas.

flow.do: Your child draws a design and labels each part and its job.
flow.say: Copy nature, or invent something new.
flow.kid: Draw guards for the robot's eyes. Label each part's job.

flow.do: Build the design on the box head. Test it with a spoon of water dripped on the forehead.
flow.say: Let's test. Where did the water go?
flow.kid: Build it. Drip water on the forehead. Did the eyes stay dry?

check.q: The water runs straight over a flat card brow and into the eyes. What should you change?
options: Curve the brow so it is higher in the middle and lower at the sides
check.why: Water runs downhill. A brow that is curved, high in the middle and low at the sides, steers drips sideways around the eyes, just like your eyebrows. Picking 'bigger eyes' would catch more drips, not fewer. Picking 'more water' changes the test, not the design.

flow.do: Improve the design once and test again.
flow.say: Engineers always test, improve and test again.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Was it better?

videos.title: How to wash your hands properly (a short, clear demonstration)
videos.why: Shows every step of handwashing, so your child can copy it after the oily hands activity.
videos.check: Not checked: find the WHO handwashing video on YouTube and check it shows all the steps, including thumbs and fingertips.

videos.title: Why do we have earwax?
videos.channel: SciShow Kids or a similar children's science channel
videos.why: Explains that earwax traps dust and moves out by itself, and why cotton buds are a bad idea.
videos.check: Not checked: search for a children's video on earwax and make sure it says not to use cotton buds.

videos.title: Body safety for children: my body belongs to me
videos.why: A calm, child-friendly video on private parts, safe and unsafe touch, and telling a trusted adult.
videos.check: Not checked: a parent should watch it first, and choose one that uses correct body names and a calm tone.

quiz.p: Which of these is an external organ?
quiz.why: Skin is on the outside and is the biggest organ. The heart, brain and stomach are internal organs, inside the body.

opts: To breathe in air and to smell
quiz.why: The nose takes in air and smells. Its hairs and mucus also trap dust.

opts: Traps dust and germs, then moves out by itself
quiz.why: Earwax is a guard. Picking 'shows the ear is dirty' is the most common idea, but clean ears make wax too.

quiz.p: What is the safe way to clean ears?
opts: Wipe the outside with a cloth
Use a cotton bud deep inside
quiz.why: Wipe only the outside. Anything pushed in can push wax deeper or hurt the eardrum.

quiz.p: Why does a haircut not hurt?
opts: The hair we see is dead. Only the root is alive.
quiz.why: The hair we see is dead cells of keratin, pushed out by a living root. Picking 'the barber is careful' misses the real reason.

quiz.p: In the sticky tape test, what were the white flakes?
quiz.why: Old skin cells flake off as new ones grow underneath. Germs are far too small to see.

quiz.p: In the bread test, which slice grew the fewest spots, apart from the untouched one?
quiz.why: Soap removed the most germs from hands. Picking 'water only' is a near miss: water removes some, but soap removes more.

quiz.p: How long should you rub your hands with soap?
quiz.why: At least 20 seconds, about Happy Birthday sung twice. Rubbing loosens the oil and germs.

quiz.p: Why is brushing at night most important?
opts: Your mouth makes less spit at night, so germs can make acid for hours
Germs only come out at night
quiz.why: Spit washes and protects teeth. At night there is less of it. Picking 'germs only come out at night' is a mix-up: germs are there all day.

quiz.p: Which is good care for the eyes?
opts: Blink and wash with clean water if dust gets in
Look at the sun to make them strong
quiz.why: Rubbing hard can scratch the eye. Never look at the sun. Only use eye drops a doctor gives.

opts: The parts covered by underwear, which are private and belong to you
Dirty parts we must not wash
Parts only doctors can talk about
quiz.why: Private parts are covered by underwear. We wash them daily. They have correct names, and they belong to you.

quiz.p: If any touch feels wrong or confusing, what should you do?
opts: Say no, get away and tell a trusted grown-up
quiz.why: Say no, get away, tell. It is never the child's fault, and secrets about touching are never kept.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
quiz.why: Scientists agree skin is an organ, hair grows and brushing helps. They still argue whether ridges are mainly for grip, feeling or both.

quiz.p: What happens in the egg test, when a plain egg sits in vinegar?
opts: Acid eats the shell and makes bubbles
quiz.why: Vinegar is an acid. It dissolves the chalky shell and gives off a gas. Mouth germs make acid that eats enamel in the same way.

quiz.p: Your left and right thumbs grew from the same genes. What are their prints like?
opts: Different: the ridge forks and ends are in different places
Exactly the same, because the genes are the same
Different, because one thumb is older
They have no pattern at all
quiz.why: Every finger has its own print. The ridges formed before birth, and tiny differences in how each fingertip grew set the details. Picking 'exactly the same' is the common idea that genes decide everything. Both thumbs are the same age, so 'older' cannot be the reason.

applications: Doctors look at skin, nails, eyes and tongue to find clues about illness.
Police use fingerprints to find out who touched something.
Phones and Aadhaar machines read fingerprints to check who a person is.
Dentists use fluoride toothpaste and sealants to protect enamel.
Hospitals have strict handwashing rules to stop germs spreading.
Tippy taps and handwashing stations in schools cut down tummy illnesses.
Sunglasses, swimming goggles and safety glasses copy the eye's guards.
Earplugs and ear muffs protect the eardrums of factory and airport workers.
Shoe soles have grooves that let water escape, the way fingertip ridges may help on wet things.
Skin grafts and burn treatments use the skin's power to renew itself.
Body safety lessons in schools help children speak up and stay safe.
Cameras on cars and buildings have hoods and wipers that keep rain off, like eyebrows and eyelids.

open_questions.q: What are fingertip ridges really for?
open_questions.why_open: Tests suggest they help us feel fine textures, and perhaps grip rough or wet things. But they may grip less on smooth dry things. Scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does each person's fingerprint pattern form in the womb?
open_questions.why_open: Ridges start at a few spots on each fingertip and spread out across it. Genes and the way the skin grows both shape where they meet. Scientists are still working out the details.
Handwashing at key times clearly helps. But we may also need to meet harmless microbes. Scientists are still studying how much, and which ones.

open_questions.q: Why do some people make dry, flaky earwax and others wet, sticky earwax?
open_questions.why_open: A difference in one gene is linked to it. Scientists are not sure why both kinds have lasted over human history.

open_questions.q: Why do humans have so little body hair compared with other apes?
open_questions.why_open: Some think it helped us cool down by sweating when running in the heat. Others have different ideas. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Why do we have eyebrows that move so much?
open_questions.why_open: They guard the eyes, and they also show feelings. Some scientists think the feelings job helped humans live in groups. It is still an idea.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many tiny living things live on your skin, and what do they all do?
open_questions.why_open: There are many kinds, different in different places on the body. Scientists are still finding out what most of them do.

jokes.j: Why did the skin feel so new?

maths.problem: A thumbnail grew 2 millimetres in two weeks. About how much will it grow in eight weeks?
maths.explain: Eight weeks is four lots of two weeks. In each two weeks, the nail grows 2 millimetres. 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8, or 4 × 2 = 8. So about 8 millimetres.
maths.context: In the Nail Tracker project, you marked your thumbnail at the skin and measured how far the mark moved as the nail grew.
maths.why_maths: Once you know how much a nail grows in a short time, multiplying tells you how much it will grow in a longer time, without waiting.

chart.title: How far the mark moved, every two weeks

maths.problem: A child has 20 milk teeth. A grown-up usually has 32 teeth. How many more teeth does the grown-up have?
maths.explain: 32 take away 20 is 12. You can check: 20 + 12 = 32. So a grown-up has 12 more teeth than a child.
maths.context: Children have 20 milk teeth. They fall out and bigger teeth grow in. A grown-up usually has 32 teeth.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells us exactly how many new teeth grow in as you grow up, which helps you notice the new ones coming.

maths.problem: Ten family members gave their right thumbprints. 6 were loops, 3 were whorls and 1 was an arch. Draw a bar chart. Which kind was most common?
maths.answer: Loops were most common, with 6 out of 10.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each kind. The loop bar is 6 tall, the whorl bar is 3 tall and the arch bar is 1 tall. The loop bar is tallest, so loops were most common. 6 + 3 + 1 = 10, so every print is counted.
maths.context: In Fingerprint Detective, you took everyone's thumbprint with pencil and tape and sorted the prints into loops, whorls and arches.
maths.why_maths: A tally and a bar chart show at a glance which pattern is most common, so you can compare your family with what scientists find.

maths.problem: A grown-up blinked 15 times in one minute. How many times would that be in 10 minutes?
maths.explain: One minute has 15 blinks. Ten minutes is ten lots of 15. 15 × 10 = 150. So about 150 blinks in 10 minutes.
maths.context: In the Blink Counter, you counted a grown-up's blinks for one minute with tally marks.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a one-minute count shows how many times the eyes are cleaned in a longer time, which is hard to count directly.

maths.problem: In the bread test, the dirty-hands slice had 12 spots and the soap slice had 3 spots. How many times as many spots did the dirty-hands slice have?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 3 is 4. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So the dirty-hands slice grew 4 times as many spots as the soap slice.
maths.context: In the bread test, hands touched slices of bread after different kinds of washing, and germs grew into spots in sealed bags.
maths.why_maths: Saying '4 times as many' tells us how much soap helps, not just that it helps.

roots.context: We have been learning about the outside of the body, from skin and hair to the ridges on your fingertips. Now we ask what your own two thumbprints tell you about how a body is made.

deep_truth.truth: Your two thumbs grew from the same genes, yet their prints had ridge forks and ends in different places. Each pattern formed before birth, shaped by tiny differences in how each fingertip grew. So your body's fine details come from how you grew, as well as from your genes.
deep_truth.habit: People often speak of genes as a complete plan of a body, drawn down to the last line. Your two thumbs carry the same genes and still have different prints, so the genes cannot hold every detail.
deep_truth.evidence: In Fingerprint Detective, your left and right thumbprints did not match, though they grew from the same genes in the same womb. Identical twins share their genes, and their fingerprints differ too. Ridges start at a few spots on each fingertip before birth and spread across it, and where they meet sets the pattern.

three.who_am_i: You are one of a kind, right down to your fingertips. Part of what makes you is the way you happened to grow.
three.what_is_life: A living body builds itself. Its cells grow and divide, and the exact shape of each part comes out of that growing.
three.what_is_this_world: Your skin meets the world all day. It keeps out dirt and germs, feels every touch, and leaves your fingerprints on what you hold.

roots.thread: Your whole body grew from one first cell. That cell divided again and again, and almost every new cell carried the same genes. Yet those cells became skin, hair, nails, eyes and ten different fingerprints. One cell with one set of genes grew into many different parts. That is one becoming many, inside your own body.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a tiny banyan seed. Inside, Shvetaketu can see nothing at all. Uddalaka tells him that the whole great banyan tree grows out of that nothing he cannot see.
teachings.link: The first cell of your body held no tiny fingerprint you could have seen. The ridges appeared only as your fingertips grew, before you were born.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, said you cannot step into the same river twice. The water is always new, yet it is still the river.
teachings.link: Your outer skin is replaced every month or two, yet the same fingerprint grows back each time, because its pattern is held in a deeper layer of skin.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in it. Nothing exists all by itself.

science.text: The top layer of skin is made of dead cells that flake off, while new cells grow underneath. The outer skin is replaced about every month or two.
Fingerprint ridges form between about 10 and 16 weeks in the womb. Genes affect what kind of pattern a finger has, but every finger's exact print is different, even between identical twins.

other_view.view: Genes matter more than this makes it sound. Identical twins' prints are often the same kind and look alike, and the kind of pattern runs in families. They would say the differences are small details, and the genes did the main work. That is an honest view.

practice.title: Read your fingertips
practice.say: Sit somewhere with good light. Hold up both hands, palms towards you. Look closely at the tip of one thumb. Follow one ridge with your eyes, from one side to the other. Now look at your other thumb in the same way. These lines grew while you were growing inside your mother. Rest your hands on your knees and take three slow breaths.
practice.kid: Hold up your hands. Look at the tip of one thumb. Follow one ridge with your eyes. Now look at your other thumb. Rest your hands. Take three slow breaths.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1847, in a big hospital in Vienna, many mothers were dying of a fever soon after giving birth. The hospital had two wards for births. In the ward run by doctors and medical students, about one mother in ten died. In the ward run by midwives, far fewer died. Most doctors blamed bad air. A young doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis, noticed a difference. The doctors often came straight from cutting open dead bodies to help with births. The midwives did not. Then his friend, Dr Jakob Kolletschka, was cut by a student's knife while examining a dead body. He died of an illness very like the mothers' fever. Semmelweis guessed that something unseen on the doctors' hands was carrying it. He made every doctor wash their hands in a chlorine solution before touching a mother. Within months, deaths in the doctors' ward fell to about one or two in a hundred. Many doctors still refused to believe him. They did not like being told their own hands carried disease. In the 1860s and 1870s, Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister showed that germs too small to see cause illness. Semmelweis had been right.
how_we_found_out.who: Ignaz Semmelweis and the midwives and doctors of the Vienna General Hospital, and later Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister
how_we_found_out.when: 1847 (handwashing in Vienna), and the 1860s and 1870s (Pasteur and Lister's work on germs)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most doctors thought the fever came from bad air, and that their own hands could not carry illness. When Semmelweis made them wash in a chlorine solution, deaths in the doctors' ward fell from about 1 in 10 to 1 or 2 in 100.
